conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-item check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days—nothing more, nothing less. Your answers are completely confidential and will help us figure out the best next steps for your emotional well-being after baby arrives. We’ll go question by question; just answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. Ready to start?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Hi Sarah… I guess I’m ready.  
Lately, when my partner or the TV tries to be funny, I mostly just feel… flat. I might force a little laugh, but it feels fake. Nothing really feels funny or light anymore—like the joy is stuck behind a wall I can’t get through.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No… not really. I mean, maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little chuckle, but it feels forced—like I’m pretending to laugh because I know I should. Mostly I just feel too tired or down to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it all feels like another chore. Sometimes I plan things, hoping the spark will come back, but when the moment arrives I’m just… numb, or I cancel because it feels too hard.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby spits up more than usual, or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right, maybe I’m just not cut out for this.” I know it’s not always my fault, but the guilt keeps circling anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, house is quiet, and suddenly my chest feels tight—like something awful is about to happen. I check if he’s breathing twenty times a night, worry the stroller might roll away by itself, imagine him choking when I’m not looking. There’s no real reason, but the fear just barges in and won’t leave.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. My heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and suddenly I’m sure something terrible is about to happen to the baby or to me—even though nothing’s going on. I’ve had to sit down and do those slow-breath things my nurse showed me just to keep from bursting into tears.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second one task is done—feeding, changing, laundry—there are three more waiting, and I’m already empty. Sometimes I just stare at the mess and cry because I don’t know where to start. I get through it, but it’s like wading through thick mud every step.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby, or I replay every little thing I think I messed up. Even when he sleeps a three-hour stretch, I’m still wide-eyed, staring at the ceiling, and then I finally drift off right before he wakes up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… sad is kind of my baseline now. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest that doesn’t lift much. Little things make me tear up—seeing other moms look happy on social media, or when my mom asks how I’m doing. Most days I just feel… gray.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried three, maybe four times this week. Sometimes it’s because the baby won’t nap and my head is pounding, other times it’s for no clear reason—just this rush of sadness that spills out. I try to do it quietly in the bathroom so my older kid doesn’t see.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my kids need.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) interview

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive self-blame/guilt  
- Daily, unprovoked anxiety, panic sensations, hypervigilance regarding infant safety  
- Overwhelm, “heavy” or “gray” emotional state, frequent crying (3–4×/wk)  
- Initial insomnia linked to ruminative worry; fatigue intensifies perceived inability to cope

Pattern  
Consistent with probable postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; no current enjoyment, tasks feel “like wading through mud.”

Risk factors  
- Depressed mood, loss of pleasure, tearfulness, guilt, sleep disturbance, anxiety/panic, impaired coping → elevated likelihood of major postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder  
- Protective factor: denies self-harm ideation (EPDS Q10 negative)

Screening observation  
Patient reports significant distress beginning post-delivery; symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning and parenting confidence. Safety: no expressed suicidal or infanticidal thoughts; no self-harm intent. Recommend formal assessment by perinatal mental health specialist to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options.
